articles.title: What Shokker Paint Booth is
articles.summary: Shokker Paint Booth designs iRacing car paints. You open your car's template, say or click what you want, watch a live preview, then render the paint file and the spec (shine) file straight into your iRacing car folder.
articles.what: iRacing reads two pictures for every car: the paint (the colours) and the spec map (how metallic, rough and glossy each pixel is). Shokker builds both for you. You describe the look with zones, finishes and patterns, or with plain words in Chat, and Shokker paints the car's template with real materials: chrome, candy, carbon, flake, pearl, colour-shift and thousands more. It works on your PC without internet; only the optional online AI chat needs a connection.
when: You want a custom iRacing livery and do not want to paint every pixel by hand.
You want metal, chrome or candy finishes that need a spec map.
You are deciding where to start.
how: Open Shokker and open your car's template with Open Paint... > Layered template (or Flat image for a flat paint).
Tell Chat what you want, or pick a colour on the car and give it a finish in PRO.
Check the live preview, then press RENDER. Shokker writes the paint and the spec into your iRacing car folder.
In iRacing, press Ctrl+R to reload the car and see it.

faq.q: Does Shokker need internet?
faq.a: No, except for the optional online AI chat.

faq.q: Does it upload my paint?
faq.a: No. You press RENDER and Ctrl+R yourself; there is no upload to Trading Paints.

faq.q: Can I paint a helmet?
faq.a: No. It paints cars only.

faq.q: What is a spec map?
faq.a: The second picture iRacing reads for metal, roughness and clearcoat.

faq.q: Is Shokker a paint program like Photoshop?
faq.a: Not exactly. Shokker paints materials for iRacing cars: it builds the paint file and the spec (shine) file from zones, finishes and patterns, and writes them to your iRacing car folder. It has basic layer and brush tools but it is not a full Photoshop replacement; it opens PSD, XCF and ORA templates but does not write them. It does not paint helmets, suits or real cars.

faq.q: Is Shokker a Photoshop-type painting tool or something different?
faq.a: Different: it paints materials (paint plus spec) for iRacing cars from zones, finishes and patterns, and writes the paint and spec files. It is not a full Photoshop replacement; it has a Photoshop round trip for that.

articles.title: How a paint gets onto your iRacing car
articles.summary: You build the look in Shokker, press RENDER, and Shokker copies a paint file and a spec file into your iRacing car folder. Then you press Ctrl+R in iRacing to load them.
articles.what: There are only five steps between your design and the sim, and each one has one job. Shokker never touches iRacing itself; it only writes two files to the folder where iRacing looks for your car's custom paint, and iRacing reads them when the car loads or when you reload textures.
when: You are not sure what happens after you press RENDER.
You are explaining the workflow to a teammate.
Your paint does not show and you want to check the chain.

Copy: the files are written into the iRacing Car Folder from the top bar: car_num_<ID>.tga or car_<ID>.tga for the paint, and car_spec_<ID>.tga for the shine. <ID> is your iRacing Customer ID.
Switch to iRacing (Alt+Tab) and be in a session with your car.
Press Ctrl+R (Reload Car Textures). The car flashes white and then shows the files on disk.

articles.title: Zones, bases, patterns, spec and finishes: the six words you need
articles.summary: A zone is where a look goes; a base is a material (a second to fifth base stack as overlays); a pattern is a visible design; a spec pattern changes only the shine; a monolithic is a complete finish; the spec map is the shine picture.
articles.what: Almost every Shokker screen uses six words. Learn them once and the rest reads easily. They are layers of the same idea: choose where (zone), choose what material (base or monolithic), add a design (pattern), add shine texture (spec pattern), and Shokker builds the spec map for iRacing.
when: A menu or helper message uses a word you do not know.
You are about to start your first design.
how: ZONE: a set of pixels plus a look. You choose the pixels by colour, by layer, by a box or a named part. Zones stack, and the zone higher in the list wins when two want the same pixel.
BASE: a plain material such as gloss, matte, satin, chrome, candy or pearl. A base changes colour and shine.
MONOLITHIC: a complete finish that brings its own colour and texture, for example a colour-shift or a carbon look. Choose it when you want the whole effect.
PATTERN: a visible design on top, such as carbon weave, stripes, camo or flames. It changes colour and only a little shine.
SPEC PATTERN: a texture for the shine only (metal flake, holographic flecks). It never changes the colour.

SPEC MAP: the second picture iRacing reads. Red is metal, green is roughness (0 is a mirror, but only chrome-tier metal, about 240 and up, can go under 15), blue is clearcoat (16 is the glossiest, 0 to 15 means none) and alpha is a lighting mask. Shokker builds it from your zones.
tips: Foundation finishes with Source colours change only the spec map and leave your paint exactly as it is.
Up to five bases can be stacked in one zone as overlays (second to fifth base).
pitfalls: A zone with a finish but no pixels shows nothing.
Do not mix up pattern (visible design) with spec pattern (shine only).

articles.title: PRO or CHAT: which door to use
articles.summary: PRO is the full tool with every control; CHAT is talking to the helper, where you type what you want. Both edit the same car and the same paint, so you can switch any time without losing work.
articles.what: The mode switch at the top has two entries: PRO and CHAT. Use PRO when you know what you want and want every control. Use CHAT when you would rather describe it. Both change the same zones and layer settings.
when: You are new and unsure which mode to use.
You want to say "retro red white and blue stripes" instead of hunting for controls.
Chat cannot do something and you need exact control.
how: PRO is the default. Everything starts here: open your template, set ID and car folder, and render.
Click CHAT in the mode switch to open the chat studio. Type what you want; your car changes and each change has an Undo.
Click PRO any time to return. Your paint and zones stay as they are; nothing is lost.
Use PRO for importing a paint, exporting to iRacing and hand painting; Chat changes zones and layer settings only.
tips: Chat works without any key: a built-in designer does a lot for free, and an online AI key only adds open-ended requests.
Say places and parts in plain words; the app names parts of the car for you.
pitfalls: Chat cannot render, save or export for you. Press RENDER yourself.

articles.title: The paint is ONE flat sheet of the whole car
articles.summary: Your paint is a single flat 2048 by 2048 picture of the car cut open, with the sides, hood, roof, trunk and bumpers lying side by side, so left and right mean the flat picture, not the car. A number or lettering that runs past a panel edge or seam is cut off there, so keep it inside one panel.
articles.what: iRacing wraps that one picture over the 3D car. That is why texture size is set per zone, why the same colour can appear on several islands, and why numbers and text are often mirrored or rotated on some islands. Every template lays the parts out differently, so always open the template of the car you drive.
when: A change appears on a part you did not expect.
Text looks backwards on one side.
You want to place something on the left door, not the left of the picture.
how: Open the template for your car and look at the SOURCE view: the islands are the parts of the car laid flat.
Use named parts when you can: a zone can choose Left side, Roof or Hood by name, so you do not have to find them on the sheet.
Check the CAR view to see where a change lands on the real car shape.
To copy a design to the other side of the car use Mirror (layer MIRROR with FLIP or ROT 90, or Mirror Mask for a zone area), then check the CAR view.
Remember a horizontal gradient runs across the whole sheet, so several islands share the same colour at the same column. Use one zone per side to fade each side separately.
tips: The size of a texture feature on the sheet is its size on the car: a 64 pixel feature is the size of a mirror.
The helper talks about places with a grid: columns A to H left to right, rows 1 to 8 top to bottom.
pitfalls: One side of the sheet may be upside down, so a copied design can land flipped; use FLIP or ROT 90.
Do not resize the canvas: iRacing needs 2048 by 2048 or 1024 by 1024.

articles.title: Your first paint in ten minutes
articles.summary: Open your car's template, give your iRacing ID and car folder once, claim an area with a colour, drop a finish on it, then RENDER and press Ctrl+R in iRacing. Training Wheels are off until you press the Tutorial button in the header; they then walk you through exactly this.
articles.what: This is the shortest path from nothing to a paint on your car. It uses the five core steps that the Tutorial also teaches. You do not need patterns, layers or spec knowledge for a first result.
when: You have never used Shokker.
You want proof that the whole chain works before you design.
how: Open your car's template: choose Open Paint... > Layered template in the top bar (layered) or Flat image (flat paint). Wait until your paint appears under SOURCE.
Type your iRacing User ID (Customer ID) and pick your car in iRacing Car Folder. These are one-time settings.
Make a zone: press Pick Color From Car in the Zone panel and click a colour on SOURCE. Click more colours to add them.
Give the zone a finish: click the BASE swatch, open Foundations > Foundation Bases, choose a base (the Tutorial suggests Chrome) and press Apply in its preview card.
Switch the template layers (Wire, Mask, Car_Mandatory) off in the Layers panel.
Press RENDER. Wait for the green Saved bar.
Alt+Tab to iRacing and press Ctrl+R in a session with your car.

articles.title: Loading a paint: flat TGA / PNG / JPEG vs a layered PSD
articles.summary: In the Open Paint menu, Layered template opens a layered template that keeps numbers, logos and body paint apart, and Flat image opens one flat picture with no layers.
articles.what: Source Paint is the file Shokker paints over. A layered template lets zones target the body only, keep sponsors safe and hide template guide layers. A flat file is fine for a quick colour change but you cannot separate the number from the body except by colour. Either way the file must be 2048 by 2048 (or 1024 by 1024).
when: You have a PSD from the car's template pack.
You only have a TGA or PNG of a finished paint.
You are not sure which button to press.
how: Open Paint... > Layered template (next to Source Paint) opens a layered Photoshop (.psd), GIMP (.xcf) or OpenRaster (.ora) file with every layer editable. Only those three types work on this button.
Open Paint... > Flat image opens a flat paint instead.
Wait for the paint to appear under SOURCE. A big PSD can take up to a minute; a message at the bottom shows progress and, at the end, how many layers loaded.
Open the template of the car you drive, at its normal 2048 by 2048 size. Do not resize it.
When you render, the template layers (Wire, Mask, Car_Mandatory and the group named Turn Off Before Exporting TGA) are left out of the car paint for you.

controls.label: Open Paint... > Flat image
controls.effect: Opens a flat paint without layers.

tips: Layer names such as Car Paint, Numbers and Sponsors let you target exactly one part.
GIMP: export as .ora or .psd, or use the .xcf directly. Krita: .ora.
After a layered PSD loads, the layer you work on starts as the first visible paintable layer, not a guide layer such as Wire.
Painting on a layer inside the Turn Off Before Exporting group shows a warning toast, and that layer will not be exported.
pitfalls: Only pixel layers import from a PSD; rasterize text and shapes first.
A file name alone in Source Paint is not enough; use the buttons so Shokker has the full path.

faq.q: Where do I find my Customer ID?

articles.title: Windows, iRacing, price and what Shokker does not do
articles.summary: Platform and limits: Shokker is for iRacing paints only: it installs on Windows and writes paint and spec files. It cannot paint a real car or wrap (that needs other software), other sims, or glow paint; Buy License opens the store page.
articles.what: Shokker Paint Booth is a Windows app: the installer is a Windows setup and there is no Mac or Linux build. It makes iRacing files only: car_<ID>.tga or car_num_<ID>.tga for the paint and car_spec_<ID>.tga for the shine. Other sims use other files and Shokker has no settings for them. A paint is a flat picture, so it cannot move, glow in the dark or change the car's shape. The licence is bought through Buy License on the licence screen, which opens the online store page (Payhip); the app itself does not show or state a price, so look at the store page. The built-in helper is free and works offline; only the optional AI uses your own key.
when: Before you buy or install.
You ask whether Shokker works on a Mac or with another sim.
You want an effect a flat paint cannot do.
how: 1. Install on a Windows PC with the Shokker setup file.
2. Activate on the licence screen. No licence yet? Press Buy License: it opens the store page; the app does not list a price itself.
3. Paint, render and drive it in iRacing. For anything not in the app, ask the helper for the nearest thing it can do.
tips: The built-in helper and design library are free; only the optional AI costs money, on your own key, with a daily cap.
pitfalls: Shokker cannot paint emissive light: iRacing has no glow-in-the-dark paint. Use a phosphorescent-looking finish instead.
Wheels and windows only change where the car's own sheet paints them.

deep.heading: Why iRacing only

Other sims expect different files, folders and spec rules, so Shokker has no export for them. You can still open a rendered TGA as a picture in another tool.

deep.heading: What a flat paint cannot do
deep.body: The paint is one flat 2048 x 2048 picture of the car cut open. It cannot animate, glow, show a 3D shape or change wheels and windows beyond what the sheet already paints. iRacing's lighting decides how chrome and flake look on track. The helper says so plainly and offers the closest real thing.

faq.q: Can you make a track or a map for me?

faq.a: No. Shokker is for iRacing paints only. Other sims expect different files, folders and spec rules, so Shokker has no export for them, and I do not promise any.

faq.q: Do I need a good graphics card?
faq.a: No. The engine renders on the processor and only uses a graphics card if the optional CuPy library is installed. The app lists no minimum PC specs.

faq.q: Can I get a refund or join a beta?
faq.a: The app does not state terms. Ask Shokker support: Settings gear > Report a Problem.

faq.q: Can I sell paints I make?
faq.a: Shokker has no shop and does not state selling rules, and this is not a legal guarantee: iRacing's and Trading Paints' own rules apply. Ask Shokker support (Settings gear > Report a Problem) before you sell anything.

faq.q: Can two people work on one paint?
faq.a: Not at the same time. Send the project or a recipe and take turns.

faq.q: Do you store my paints, and can other people see them?
faq.a: Your paints stay as files on your own PC (your saved project and the files in your iRacing car folder); Shokker has no account-based cloud storage or shop. Other drivers see a paint only if you put it on Trading Paints, because iRacing never sends textures between drivers. The built-in helper sends nothing out; with an AI key the online model gets a text summary and sometimes the preview.

faq.q: Can I sell the paints I make on Trading Paints?
faq.a: Shokker has no shop and does not state selling rules, and I cannot give a legal guarantee. Check the rules of iRacing and of Trading Paints, then ask Shokker support (Settings gear > Report a Problem) before you sell anything.

faq.q: I want my money back
faq.a: I am sorry it went wrong. I cannot grant refunds and the app does not state refund terms, so contact Shokker support: Settings gear > Report a Problem gathers the details to send. Tell me what went wrong first, such as a paint that does not show or a render that fails, and I can usually fix it.

faq.q: How do I send my paint to a teammate or another PC?
faq.a: For continued editing, keep both the saved .spbproj and unchanged original source PSD or paint; reopening checks the recorded source path and fingerprint. For a look, use Share Recipe or SAVE SHOKK. For finished paint, send the rendered paint/spec files or Export ZIP Package. Those rendered files do not preserve editable layers.

Tell me what went wrong, such as a paint that does not show in iRacing or a render that fails, and I will try to fix it first.

faq.q: Am I allowed to sell the paints I create with this app?
faq.a: Shokker has no shop and does not state selling rules, and I cannot give a legal guarantee: iRacing and Trading Paints rules apply. Ask Shokker support (Settings gear > Report a Problem) before you sell anything.

articles.title: iRacing side questions: owning the car, pit stall banners and iRacing's own shop
articles.summary: Shokker writes car paint and spec files, and iRacing only reads them once it has made the car's paint folder, which happens the first time you run that car in a session. Pit stall banners, interiors and iRacing's own store are outside what Shokker writes.
articles.what: Shokker can open any car template you have, but iRacing reads a paint from the car's folder inside the iRacing paint folder in Documents, and iRacing creates that folder the first time you run the car in a race or test session. So to see your paint on the car you need to run it in iRacing at least once (what iRacing lets you run is up to iRacing). Shokker writes the car's paint (car_<ID>.tga or car_num_<ID>.tga) and spec (car_spec_<ID>.tga) only; helmet and suit folders, pit stall banners, interiors and other iRacing items are not Shokker targets. Shokker has no shop, and submitting a paint to iRacing's own store is not something the app does. Other drivers see your paint through the Trading Paints service.
when: You want to paint a car you have not run in iRacing yet.
You want a pit stall banner or another non-car item.
You want to sell or submit a paint through iRacing.
how: 1. Run the car once in an iRacing test session so iRacing creates its paint folder.
2. In Shokker, set iRacing Car Folder to that folder and your iRacing User ID at the top.
3. Paint, render, then press Ctrl+R in iRacing to reload.
4. To let others see it, upload it to Trading Paints (paint as TGA or PNG, spec as the .mip iRacing builds).
5. For items Shokker does not write (pit stall, interior), use iRacing's own paint shop or another editor.
tips: The car folder name is the car's path with a space instead of the slash, for example stockcars chevyss; iRacing's paint shop tool-tip shows it.
pitfalls: Painting a car whose folder iRacing has not created yet means the render has no iRacing folder to be copied into, and a mistyped car folder can end up saving into its parent folder where iRacing never looks.
Helmet and suit paints use their own iRacing folders; Shokker's render does not write them.

Pit stall banners, interiors, helmets and suits, and iRacing's own store all live outside that. iRacing never sends paint files between drivers; other people see your paint only through Trading Paints.

faq.a: Shokker has no shop and does not submit paints anywhere.

faq.q: Am I limited to the cars I own, or does the app allow any model?
faq.a: Shokker does not check ownership and opens any car template. To see the paint in iRacing you must run that car once so iRacing creates its paint folder; whether you can run a car you do not own is up to iRacing.

mistakes.symptom: There is no folder for the car to pick.
mistakes.cause: iRacing has not created it yet.
mistakes.fix: Run the car once in a test session, then pick its folder.

mistakes.symptom: Friends do not see the paint.
mistakes.cause: iRacing does not share paint files.
mistakes.fix: Upload it to Trading Paints.

protips: Run a quick test session in any new car before painting it, so the folder exists when you first render.

articles.title: Rain and wet tracks: what your paint and spec do
articles.summary: Shokker writes one paint and one spec map, with no rain or wet-weather version, and its preview cannot show rain. For a car that always looks wet, use the Wet Look finish or the CC Wet Zone spec overlay.
articles.what: A render writes the paint (car_num_ID.tga or car_ID.tga) and one spec map (car_spec_ID.tga). There is no second spec for wet weather and no rain setting in Shokker, so iRacing uses the same two files in every session. How water, spray and wet light look on the car is up to iRacing, and Shokker's live preview cannot show it. What you can control is how glossy the car is all the time: a low roughness and the glossiest clearcoat (16) give the tightest, wettest highlight.
when: You race in the rain and wonder whether you need a different spec.
You want the car to look wet or freshly washed.
Your car looks different on a wet track than in Shokker.
how: 1. For a permanently wet shine, make a zone on the body and pick Wet Look under Base Material.
2. For uneven wet-looking clear patches, add the CC Wet Zone spec overlay to that zone.
3. In the spec, keep roughness (G) low and the clearcoat (B) at 16, the glossiest value.
4. Press RENDER, then Ctrl+R in iRacing; judge it in a dry and a wet session, because Shokker cannot show rain.
tips: Gloss reads stronger when the colour underneath is deep; very light colours hide a wet highlight.
pitfalls: There is no wet-weather spec file to make: renaming a copy of the spec does nothing.
The preview is a flat picture of the sheet; weather never shows there.
aliases: does my paint change in the rain

deep.heading: One spec for every weather
deep.body: Shokker writes exactly two files per render: the paint and the spec map. iRacing loads them whatever the weather, so there is nothing extra to make for a wet race. Weather effects on the car come from iRacing, not from the paint files.

deep.heading: Making the car look wet
deep.body: A wet look is a tight, deep highlight, which comes from low roughness and the glossiest clearcoat. The Wet Look finish is built for that. The CC Wet Zone overlay adds slightly uneven glossy clear patches that read like real water on the clear.

examples.goal: Looks freshly washed in every session
examples.result: A razor-sharp gloss highlight on the whole body.

examples.title: Patchy wet clear
examples.goal: Uneven water-on-clear look
examples.result: Glossier patches across the clear, visible in the reflections.

faq.q: Do I need a different spec map for rain?
faq.a: No. Shokker writes one spec map and iRacing uses it in every session.

faq.q: Can Shokker show how my car looks in the rain?
faq.a: No. The preview cannot show weather; check it in iRacing.

faq.q: How do I make the car look wet all the time?
faq.a: Use the Wet Look finish, or add the CC Wet Zone spec overlay to a glossy finish.

mistakes.symptom: The car looks dull on a wet track.
mistakes.cause: A rough or satin finish stays rough in every weather.
mistakes.fix: Lower the roughness or use Wet Look for a glossier car.

mistakes.symptom: A second spec file made for rain does nothing.
mistakes.cause: iRacing reads only car_spec with your ID.
mistakes.fix: Keep one spec map; change its gloss instead.

protips: Judge gloss in a dry session first; if it reads wet in the sun it will still read glossy in the rain.

articles.title: Crash damage and your paint
articles.summary: Shokker has no crash-damage paint and writes no damage files: a render is one paint and one spec map, and what a crash does to the car is up to iRacing. For a car that already looks battle-worn, use a worn finish such as Hardware: Battle Worn, Sun Faded, Die-Back Patina or Extreme: BMX Dirt.
articles.what: Every render writes the same two files, the paint and the spec map, and iRacing loads them as they are. Shokker has no setting for dents, scrapes or broken parts and cannot make the paint change after contact. What it can do is make the paint look used from the start: worn finishes bake chips, fading and rough clear into the look, and spec overlays add uneven clearcoat. That look is the same in every lap of every session.
when: You want visible damage or scrapes on the car.
You want a battle-worn or rat-rod look.
You wonder whether your paint changes after a crash.
how: 1. Make a zone on the body (or only the panels you want worn).
2. Under BASE press Base Material and search worn, patina or dirt; pick Hardware: Battle Worn, Sun Faded, Die-Back Patina or Extreme: BMX Dirt.
3. Lower Base Strength to let some of your own paint show through.
4. Keep sponsors and numbers clear of the heaviest wear, then RENDER.
tips: Wear looks real at edges and lower panels; keep the roof and hood cleaner.
pitfalls: Too much wear hides your sponsors and numbers.
A worn finish is permanent in the file; it does not appear or grow during a race.

deep.heading: What the files can and cannot do
deep.body: The paint and spec map are still pictures. They decide the colours and the shine, not how the car reacts to a crash. Anything that changes during a session comes from iRacing, so there is nothing in Shokker to switch on for damage.

deep.heading: Faking a hard season
deep.body: Worn finishes give chipped edges, faded colour and a duller clear. Pair them with a strong base colour at reduced Base Strength so the livery still reads, and keep the wear off logos so sponsors stay legible.

examples.result: Worn-through edges over your colours.

examples.goal: Dirty lower body
examples.result: Dirt on the lower body, clean above.

faq.q: Can I paint crash damage?
faq.a: Not as damage: Shokker writes no damage files. You can paint a worn look that is always there.

faq.q: Does my paint change when I crash?
faq.a: Not from anything Shokker writes; any damage you see in a session is iRacing's.

faq.q: Which finishes look battle-worn?
faq.a: Hardware: Battle Worn, Sun Faded, Die-Back Patina and Extreme: BMX Dirt.

mistakes.symptom: The sponsors disappeared under the wear.
mistakes.cause: The worn finish covers the logo areas.
mistakes.fix: Lower Base Strength or keep the worn zone off the logos.

mistakes.symptom: The whole car looks dirty.
mistakes.cause: Extreme: BMX Dirt is on the body zone.
mistakes.fix: Put it on a zone over the lower sides only.

protips: Wear reads best on a few edges and lower panels; a fully worn car just looks dirty.

articles.title: Seeing the car in 3D, and 3D model export
articles.summary: Honest limits: Shokker is paint only, with no 3D car view and no 3D model or printable mesh export, and it cannot change the car shape; its live preview shows the flat sheet. Render and look at it in iRacing, whose 3D Car Viewer reloads a saved paint.
articles.what: Shokker edits the flat 2048 by 2048 sheet and shows it flat in the LIVE PREVIEW. There is no 3D view, no painting on a 3D model and no 3D model export (no OBJ, FBX or GLB). What Shokker can export are pictures: the paint and spec TGA files, a PNG, and the Photoshop round trip. To see your design on the car, press RENDER, then use iRacing: its 3D Car Viewer in My Content reloads a saved paint by itself, and in a session Ctrl+R reloads the car textures.
when: You want to check the paint on the car before racing.
You want a 3D file of the car for Blender or a render.
You want to paint directly on a 3D car.
how: 1. Set your iRacing User ID and the car folder at the top, then press RENDER.
2. In iRacing open My Content and the 3D Car Viewer: it reloads the saved paint by itself.
3. Or join a test session in the car and press Ctrl+R to reload the textures.
4. Change the design in Shokker, render again and look again; the viewer shows whatever files are in the folder.
tips: Turn the car in iRacing's viewer to check the seams where the sides meet the hood and bumpers; the flat sheet hides them.
pitfalls: The live preview is flat: patterns that change the spec are subtle there and show properly only on the 3D car in iRacing.
In a replay iRacing does not reload cars sitting in their pit stalls; move to a moment when your car is on track.

deep.heading: Why the preview is flat
deep.body: The iRacing paint is a flat sheet that iRacing wraps onto its own 3D car. Shokker works on that sheet directly, so its preview is the sheet. The 3D model belongs to iRacing and is not something Shokker has or exports.

deep.heading: The quickest 3D check
deep.body: Render, then keep iRacing's 3D Car Viewer open in My Content: it reloads the saved paint by itself, so each new render shows up without restarting. In a session, Ctrl+R does the same; the car flashes white and then shows the new files.

examples.goal: See the stripe line up across hood and roof
examples.result: You see the paint on the real car shape and can fix any mismatch.

examples.title: Show the design to a team mate
examples.goal: Share a picture, not a model

settings.Shokker: Export PNG or the Photoshop round trip

faq.q: Can I see my car in 3D in Shokker?
faq.a: No. Render and look at it in iRacing's 3D Car Viewer, or press Ctrl+R in a session.

faq.q: Can I export a 3D model of the car?
faq.a: No. Shokker exports pictures (TGA, PNG and the Photoshop round trip), not 3D files.

faq.q: Can I paint directly on a 3D car?
faq.a: No. You paint the flat sheet; iRacing wraps it onto the car.

mistakes.symptom: The 3D viewer shows the old paint.
mistakes.cause: The render did not reach the car folder, or the folder is for another car.
mistakes.fix: Check the car folder and User ID at the top and render again.

mistakes.symptom: A spec pattern looks invisible.
mistakes.cause: Spec patterns are subtle in the flat preview.
mistakes.fix: Judge them on the 3D car in iRacing.

protips: Keep iRacing's 3D Car Viewer open next to Shokker while you design; every render is one glance away.
